deep.reconstruction:
The page is dated Jan. 18, 1797 and has three independent pieces.

(1) PRODUCT OF TWO 'CUBIC' INTEGRALS. Gauss expands the product of
A(x) = ∫_0^x t dt/(1-t^3)^{1/3} and B(x) = ∫_0^x dt/(1-t^3)^{2/3}.
[My steps:] Expand the integrands binomially with coefficients (1/3)_n/n! and (2/3)_n/n!, then integrate term by term:
A = x^2/2 + x^5/15 + x^8/36 + 14x^11/891 + 5x^14/486 + ...
B = x + x^4/6 + 5x^7/63 + 4x^10/81 + 110x^13/3159 + ...
Multiplying gives
A·B = (1/2)x^3 + (3/20)x^6 + (11/140)x^9 + (31/616)x^12 + (717/20020)x^15 + ...
Gauss writes 1/2, 3/20, 11/140, an inserted '(+31/770 x^12)', and 3·239/(220·91) x^15.

Context [my interpretation]. On the Fermat cubic x^3+y^3=1, dx/y^2 is the differential of the first kind and x dx/y is a differential of the second kind. The complete integrals (0 to 1) are B(2/3,2/3)/3 and B(1/3,1/3)/3. Their product is Γ(1/3)Γ(2/3)/3 = 2π/(3√3) ≈ 1.2092, which is a Euler-type identity. The partial sums of Gauss's series at x=1 (0.5 + 0.15 + 0.0786 + 0.0503 + 0.0358 + ...) creep toward this value. So he is probably examining this Euler/Legendre-type product, an analogue of his lemniscatic work of January 1797.

The next line reads: = CC' + C∫x dx/(1-x^3)^{1/3} + C'∫dx/(1-x^3)^{2/3}. This looks like an attempt to express the product through constants C, C' (complete values?) and the two integrals. As written it does not match the naive expansion (C+A)(C'+B), which pairs C with B, so its exact intent is unclear.

A struck-out series follows (½x^3 + 3/28 x^6 + 9/140 x^9 ...). Below it is a line '−(1 * + 1/140 x^6 + 1/140 x^9 ...'. These appear to be a discarded variant or a difference series; I cannot securely reconstruct them.

(2) EULER-TYPE PRODUCT OVER PRIMES VERSUS PRODUCT OVER ODD MULTIPLES OF π.
The first product is P(x) = (1 - x/2)(1 + x/3)(1 - x/5)(1 + x/7)(1 + x/11)(1 - x/13)... over the primes. For odd p the factor is (1 - χ(p)x/p), where χ is the character mod 4; the factor for p=2 is (1 - x/2).
The linear coefficient is S1 = -(1/2 + Σ_{p odd} χ(p)/p). Euler's 1775 series gives 1/3 - 1/5 + 1/7 + 1/11 - 1/13 - ... ≈ 0.3349813, so |S1| = 0.5 - 0.3349813 = 0.1650187. Gauss writes 0,1650188.
The quadratic coefficient of the product itself is e2 = (S1^2 - Σ_p 1/p^2)/2 = (0.0272312 - 0.4522474)/2 = -0.2125081. Gauss writes 0,21250[blot]1, i.e. very plausibly 0,2125081.
The signs in the image appear as '−+' (sign changed or ambiguous). The numbers fit the expansion of the product, 1 - 0.1650188x - 0.2125081x^2. They do not fit its reciprocal: the reciprocal's x^2 coefficient would be (S1^2 + ΣP^-2)/2 ≈ 0.2397.

As a model he expands (1 - x/π)(1 + x/(3π))(1 - x/(5π))... = 1 - x/4 - x^2/32 - ....
[My steps:]
- Linear term: -(1/π)(1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - ...) = -1/4.
- Quadratic term: ((1/4)^2 - (1/π^2)(π^2/8))/2 = -1/32.
Indeed the zeros are π, -3π, 5π, -7π, ..., so the product equals cos(x/4) - sin(x/4) [my identification]. He is thus comparing a prime 'Euler product' with signs from p mod 4 against its elementary analogue over the odd numbers. At x=1 the odd-prime part gives L(1,χ_4) = π/4.

(3) LAPLACE ON SINGULAR SOLUTIONS. Gauss notes 'La Place demonstrait': if μ = 0 is a particular (singular) solution of dy = p dx, then μ is a common divisor of p + (∂²p/∂x∂y)/(∂²p/∂y²) and 1/(∂p/∂y).
[My check:] Along a singular solution ∂p/∂y = ∞, i.e. 1/p_y = 0. For the curve 1/p_y = 0 to be an integral curve, we need (1/p_y)_x + p(1/p_y)_y = 0, i.e. p + p_xy/p_yy = 0. The next page extends this to second-order equations.

Margins: rotated names (probably people or book list) and scattered arithmetic, unrelated or unidentifiable.
errors: The x^12 coefficient of A·B is 31/616 (≈0.05032), not 31/770 as the inserted term appears to read. All other coefficients (1/2, 3/20, 11/140, 3·239/(220·91) = 717/20020) are correct. Either a slip by Gauss or a misreading of '616'.

The prime-product line is headed (in the transcription) by '1/(...)'. However, the quadratic coefficient 0.2125081 equals the x^2 coefficient (in absolute value) of the product ∏(1±x/p) itself, not of its reciprocal (which would be ≈0.2397). Signs are ambiguous ('−+') in the image.
The relation 'A·B = CC' + C∫x dx/(1-x^3)^{1/3} + C'∫dx/(1-x^3)^{2/3}' is not an identity as it stands; its intended meaning (complementary integrals, constants of integration) is unclear.
The struck-out series (3/28, 9/140, ...) and the line '−(1 * + 1/140 x^6 + 1/140 x^9' do not match the correct coefficients and appear abandoned.

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine calculations. The integral product is Euler's beta-type identity, computed in the month Gauss began his lemniscate work. The prime product uses Euler's published values of Σ±1/p and Σ1/p^2. Mildly notable is that in January 1797 Gauss was numerically treating an Euler product over primes, with signs from p mod 4, side by side with its trigonometric analogue. This is an early look at L(s,χ_4)-type objects, but nothing beyond Euler's results.
